prompt:
以下はある英語ニュースpodcast記事のFull Story・Point One・Point Twoです。
Point One・Point Twoそれぞれについて、以下6項目を判定してください
(それぞれPASS/FAIL)。

- qa_not_caveat_only: このPointが、研究上の限界・一般化上の注意・免責事項
  だけで構成されていない場合PASS(それらに加えて実質的な新しい内容がある
  場合もPASS。留保だけでPoint枠全体が終わっている場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_full_story_paraphrase: Full Storyの要約・言い換えに留まっていない
  場合PASS(Full Storyの中心的なlogic・結論を語彙だけ変えて繰り返している
  場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_other_point_paraphrase: もう一方のPointの要約・言い換えになって
  いない場合PASS
- qa_explains_why_it_matters: 「だから何なのか」を具体的に説明できている
  場合PASS(聞き手にとっての具体的な意味・示唆がある場合)
- qa_specific_not_generic: この記事のLedger固有の内容に基づいており、他の
  どんな記事にもほぼそのまま流用できる一般論になっていない場合PASS
- qa_adds_new_value: 新しい理解・解釈・意外性・具体的示唆のいずれかを
  実際に加えている場合PASS(Full Storyだけを聞いた場合と比べて、聞き手の
  理解が実際に深まっている場合)

reasoningには、判定理由を1〜2文の日本語で書いてください(特にFAILの場合は
具体的な理由を明記してください)。

【Full Story】
The newest part of this story is not simply that satellites can be attacked. That has been shown before. The more precise question is: has a weapon itself been placed in orbit?

On September 14, 2026, U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the United States was deploying space-control weapons in orbit. He said they were meant to protect the joint force from hostile actions. The next day, an official U.S. Space Force article called this the first acknowledgment that the Space Force had put weapons in orbit.

But the statement was limited. It did not name the system, explain its exact attack method, or identify a target. So the confirmed news is the official acknowledgment of orbit-based weapons, not a full description of what they can do.

This is different from the many satellites used for GPS, missile warning, tracking, and communication. Those missions can support or protect space systems. They are not, by themselves, proof that an attack weapon is in orbit.

Other claims need the same care. A 2025 U.S. intelligence assessment said Russia was developing a satellite with a nuclear weapon as an anti-satellite capability. It did not say that the satellite had been launched, deployed, or used.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit or on celestial bodies. It also bans military bases and weapons tests on the Moon and other celestial bodies. But it does not ban every weapon in space. UN votes in 2024 and 2025 showed continuing concern about an arms race, but they did not create a broad new treaty banning all space weapons.

【Point One】
Here is the useful boundary. Russia in 2021, China in 2007, and India in 2019 destroyed satellites with missiles fired from Earth. That showed a ground attack, not a weapon left in orbit. HBTSS, GPS, missile-warning, tracking, and resilience systems have support or protection missions. The new point is the official claim of a weapon in orbit—not every military satellite.

【Point Two】
Counterspace can affect a satellite, the signal between it and users, or equipment on the ground. It can include electronic interference and cyberattacks. In 2022, a cyberattack on the KA-SAT network disrupted users; the EU blamed Russia, but the satellite was not destroyed. In May 2026, four Russian military satellites moved near a Western commercial radar satellite, with no confirmed attack or purpose. A reported Russian pellet system remains an unverified development story, not a tested or deployed weapon.

point_one.reasoning: ロシア・中国・インドによる地上発射ミサイル攻撃や、HBTSSなど具体的な事例を加え、「攻撃能力があること」と「兵器を軌道上に置くこと」の違いを明確にしている。Full Storyの中心結論と重なる部分はあるが、具体例によって新しい公式発表の意味を判別する基準を実質的に与えている。

point_two.reasoning: カウンタースペース活動を衛星本体・通信経路・地上設備への作用に分け、KA-SATへのサイバー攻撃、ロシア衛星の接近、未検証のペレット兵器という具体例を示している。これにより、衛星を破壊しなくても攻撃や妨害が成立し得る一方、接近や報道だけでは攻撃確認にならないという実務的な読み方が加わる。
